description:
We are a Franco-Turkish, women-led team passionate about geospatial technologies, Earth observation and the power of satellite data to better understand our planet.

With backgrounds and interests in GIS, remote sensing, spatial analysis and satellite imagery, we are excited to explore innovative ways of turning geospatial data into meaningful insights and real-world solutions. We enjoy combining technical curiosity, creativity and different perspectives to tackle challenges.
summary:
Burning Activity Atlas creates a consistent global record of fire activity from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations, covering 2003–2025.

Although both sensors detect active fires, they differ in spatial resolution and detection capabilities. VIIRS typically reports many more hotspots than MODIS. Directly combining their observations would therefore introduce artificial changes into long-term fire records.

Our project addresses this problem through a statistical harmonization method. Using their overlapping observation period (2012–2019), we calculate hierarchical conversion factors to bring MODIS detections onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale. We then apply these factors to build a continuous record, while testing its performance on observations the calibration did not use.

The result is an interactive global atlas featuring historical fire activity, sensor comparisons and a Burning Activity Calendar to explore seasonal patterns and anomalies.

By making observations from different satellite generations more comparable, Burning Activity Atlas supports a better understanding of long-term changes in global fire activity.
details:
What does the project do?

Burning Activity Atlas combines NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP) into a comparable global fire-activity record covering 2003–2025.

The project consists of two main components:

  • A Python processing pipeline that quality-controls, aggregates and harmonizes satellite observations.
  • An interactive web atlas that allows users to explore fire activity, compare sensors, visualize historical trends and investigate monthly anomalies.

Here is the link to our github: https://github.com/GeoByteBrew/BurningActivityAtlas.git

Benefits and intended impact

The main benefit is a continuous, VIIRS-equivalent time series covering both the long MODIS era and the VIIRS era, without mixing incompatible sensor detection counts.

Researchers, students and other users can identify discrepancies between sensors, assess how statistical conversion improves comparability, and detect recent deviations from historical fire-activity patterns.

The atlas makes these analyses accessible through a progressive approach: from a global overview to regional and country-level comparisons, and finally to local fire-activity patterns. Its intended impact is to support more consistent monitoring of fire activity across geographical areas and over time.

How does the harmonization work?

MODIS and VIIRS do not detect the same number of hotspots. VIIRS has a finer spatial resolution (375 m compared with approximately 1 km for MODIS) and generally reports more detections.

Rather than degrading VIIRS to the MODIS scale, we chose VIIRS S-NPP as our reference and statistically convert MODIS observations to an equivalent scale.

Conversion factors are estimated from the overlapping observation period (2012–2019), using a hierarchical approach:

World → UN sub-region → Country → 5 km cell → Cell-month

Factors are calculated separately for daytime and nighttime observations. A shrinkage parameter (K = 50) allows estimates based on limited observations to rely more heavily on broader geographical levels, reducing instability in sparse areas.

The final record uses one source at a time: actual VIIRS observations when available, or converted MODIS observations when VIIRS is unavailable. The sensors are never simply added together.

We also identify 24 platform outages using known outage information and global daily detection patterns, preventing missing observations from being interpreted as days without fire.

Key methodological decisions

  • Statistical conversion: We use ratios of detection totals rather than a more complex regression model. This approach is transparent, computationally efficient and suitable for sparse fire-detection data.
  • One VIIRS reference platform: We selected Suomi-NPP because it provides the longest VIIRS record overlapping with MODIS. NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 were not included in the published global run.
  • Orbit drift assessment: MODIS calibration uses 2012–2019 as its reference period. Terra and Aqua overpass-time changes are monitored in subsequent years to assess temporal stability.
  • Scalable processing: We downloaded NASA FIRMS yearly country archives instead of relying on the API, which would require several hundred thousand requests for a global, multi-year dataset. The raw archives are processed locally because of their size and are not hosted directly on GitHub.
  • Progressive testing: Development followed several stages: synthetic tests, a regional pilot, a global one-year run and finally the full global multi-year dataset.

Results and validation

The global Terra+Aqua conversion factor is 4.05 (90% interval: 4.01–4.10), with separate daytime and nighttime factors of 3.48 and 8.87, respectively.

On held-out months within the calibration period, raw MODIS totals represent approximately 24% of VIIRS detections. After conversion, they reach approximately 98% of the VIIRS total. The correlation between converted MODIS and observed VIIRS regional monthly patterns is approximately 1.00.

During the 2020–2025 temporal assessment, the annual converted-to-VIIRS ratio remains between 0.94 and 1.01, indicating that the conversion remains relatively stable beyond the calibration period.

The interactive atlas

The web application is designed to provide a progressive exploration of global fire activity:

  • Global overview: A worldwide visualization using 50 km grid cells, providing an overview of global fire-activity patterns.
  • Geographical filters: Users can focus their analysis on UN sub-regions and individual countries.
  • Progressive geographical exploration: Users can navigate from a UN sub-region to an individual country. When a country is selected, the visualization switches to a finer 25 km grid, allowing more detailed analysis of national fire-activity patterns.
  • Regional case studies: Selected study areas (Iberia, California, Central Africa and South-East Australia) provide access to higher-resolution visualizations using 10 km and 5 km grid cells, enabling more detailed investigations of local fire-activity patterns.
  • Sensor comparison: Users can compare raw MODIS, raw VIIRS and the harmonized record.
  • Historical analysis: A Burning Activity Calendar and maps showing deviations from historical normal conditions.
  • Local analysis: Users can draw or upload an area of interest to investigate fire activity within a selected geographical extent.
  • Method explanations: Dedicated explanations help users understand the harmonization process and interpret the results.

Four regional detail views—Iberia, California, Central Africa and South-East Australia—illustrate different geographical contexts and fire regimes. The underlying harmonization is global and is not limited to these selected regions.

Creativity and team considerations

Creativity lies in both the statistical approach and the design of the final product.

The project addresses the challenge of comparing observations from sensors with different spatial resolutions through a transparent, hierarchical conversion method. On the application side, progressive Level of Detail (LOD) makes it possible to explore a global dataset in a browser while maintaining access to increasingly detailed geographical information.

Comparative maps and charts also make the differences between raw sensor observations, converted observations and residual discrepancies easier to understand.

As a team, we prioritized scientific reliability, reproducibility and accessibility over visual complexity. Key decisions included selecting one reference sensor, validating the methodology before scaling up, using reproducible NASA FIRMS archives and explicitly communicating the method's limitations.

Limitations and future work

The method improves comparability at regional, monthly and yearly scales, but does not reconstruct individual VIIRS hotspots. In fact, in 54% of cell-months with VIIRS detections, MODIS recorded no fire. This illustrates an important limitation of statistical harmonization: comparable aggregate totals do not imply that individual detections can be recovered.

Converted totals also remain approximately 5% below VIIRS during the calibration period.

Future work includes external validation against burned-area products, improving performance in regions with systematic biases, and integrating NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 using their actual observations.

Tools and technologies

  • Satellite data: NASA FIRMS — MODIS MCD14ML Collection 6.1 and VIIRS VNP14IMG (Suomi-NPP).
  • Data processing: Python, pandas, GeoPandas, NumPy, PyArrow, pyproj, Shapely and matplotlib.
  • Web application: React, TypeScript, CesiumJS and Vite.
  • Geospatial framework: EPSG:6933 global equal-area grid and Natural Earth administrative boundaries.

AI assistants were used to support coding and documentation. All scientific values and results are calculated from NASA FIRMS satellite data through the project's processing pipeline; none are AI-generated.
